title: Earnings Desk: real quarters
teaches: Read real quarters the way a desk does: put the company's own numbers against the consensus, call beat, miss or in line, work the surprise in percent, then read the guide and the rest of the report, because a beat does not promise a rally and a miss does not promise a drop.

facts.quote: A company beats (exceeds) the estimate or misses (falls short of) the estimate based on how actual earnings or revenues compare to the consensus. If the number equals the estimate, it’s said to be in line.

walkthroughs.title: Two numbers, one verdict
steps: Every quarter, put two numbers side by side. First, the company's own, most often in a press release filed with an 8-K.
Second, the consensus: the average of what the analysts expect.
Above it, a beat. Below, a miss. Right on it, in line.
Then work the surprise: actual minus consensus, divided by the consensus, times 100.

walkthroughs.title: Netflix, April 2022
steps: Netflix earns $3.53 a share against a $2.89 consensus. A clean EPS beat.
But it loses 0.2 million paid members, when its own forecast called for adding 2.5 million.
Then it guides to losing 2 million more next quarter. The stock drops 35% in one day.
The beat was the quarter that's gone. Members and the guide were what's coming. That's what traded.

walkthroughs.title: Meta, February 2023
steps: Meta reports EPS of $1.76. Analysts wanted $2.22. Looks like a miss.
But $4.20 billion of restructuring charges sit inside that number. Take them out and EPS is $1.24 higher.
Revenue beats. The 2023 cost outlook comes down. The buyback grows by $40 billion.
The stock closes up 23% the next day. Read the whole release, not one line.

questions.q: Netflix, first quarter 2022: EPS $3.53. Refinitiv consensus $2.89. Same quarter last year, $3.75. How do you read EPS?
choices: A beat, it's over the consensus
A miss, it's under the consensus
A miss, it's under last year
questions.answer: A beat, it's over the consensus
questions.why: A beat. The only bar for beat or miss is the consensus, the average of what the analysts covering the stock expect. $3.53 against $2.89 clears it by a lot. Last year's $3.75 is a growth question, not a beat-or-miss one. One thing I'd flag before you get excited: Netflix says the $3.53 held a $162 million non-cash currency gain. The beat's real, but I wouldn't take its size at face value.
questions.lesson_line: Beat or miss is always against the consensus. Last year is a different question.

wrong.A miss, it's under the consensus: Backwards. $3.53 sits above $2.89, not under it.
wrong.In line, close to consensus: In line means it matched the estimate. $3.53 against $2.89 isn't close.
wrong.A miss, it's under last year: It is under last year's $3.75. But that's growth. Beat or miss gets judged against the consensus.

questions.simple: A beat, because $3.53 is above the $2.89 the analysts expected.

questions.q: Walmart, first quarter of fiscal 2023: adjusted EPS of $1.30. Analysts were looking for $1.48. That's a beat.
questions.why: False. That's a miss, and a big one. $1.30 is under the $1.48 the Street wanted. CNBC said Walmart missed by a wide margin, and AP's Zacks survey had it far short of $1.48 too. Get the direction right first. Everything else you read in the report hangs off it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the consensus is a miss. Nail the direction before you read anything else.
questions.simple: False. $1.30 is under the $1.48 analysts expected, so it's a miss.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Actual EPS minus the consensus, divided by the consensus, times 100, is the earnings ___ in percent.
questions.why: Surprise. Zacks works it as actual minus consensus, over the consensus, times 100. Positive is a beat, negative a miss. When a loss is expected, Zacks divides by the consensus without its minus sign.
questions.lesson_line: The surprise in percent puts a beat at Netflix and a miss at Walmart on the same scale.

questions.q: Alphabet, first quarter 2024: EPS $1.89 vs $1.51 expected. Revenue $80.54 billion vs $78.59 billion expected. What's the read?
questions.why: Beat on EPS and revenue. EPS of $1.89 cleared the $1.51 LSEG estimate. Revenue of $80.54 billion cleared $78.59 billion. Reuters called it a beat on sales and profit too. You read each line on its own, against its own estimate, because they don't always agree. When they split, that's where the story is. Growth is a separate check: sales were up 15% on a year ago. That's the kind of report I want behind a stock I own.
questions.lesson_line: EPS and revenue are two lines. Each one beats or misses on its own.

wrong.EPS beat, revenue missed: Revenue beat too: $80.54 billion against $78.59 billion expected.
wrong.In line on both lines: In line means it matched the estimate. Both numbers came in well above it.

questions.simple: A beat on both, because $1.89 is over $1.51 and $80.54 billion is over $78.59 billion.

questions.q: Target, first quarter 2022: adjusted EPS $2.19 vs $3.07 expected. Revenue $25.17 billion vs $24.49 billion expected. How does it read?
questions.why: EPS missed, revenue beat. Adjusted EPS of $2.19 came in 88 cents short of the $3.07 consensus. That's a big hole. Revenue of $25.17 billion topped the $24.49 billion expected, and AP's FactSet poll makes the same two calls. So people kept shopping at Target, and the money got lost between the register and the bottom line. When the lines split, say both halves out loud. Then go find out why they split.
questions.lesson_line: A sales beat and a profit miss can sit in one report. Say both halves, then find out why.

wrong.EPS beat, revenue missed: That's backwards. $2.19 is below $3.07, and $25.17 billion is above $24.49 billion.
wrong.Missed on EPS and revenue: Revenue beat: $25.17 billion against $24.49 billion expected.

questions.simple: EPS missed and revenue beat, because $2.19 is under $3.07 while $25.17 billion is over $24.49 billion.

questions.q: The 'expected' number in an earnings headline can change depending on which analyst survey the story quotes.
questions.why: True. Refinitiv, FactSet and StreetAccount each run their own survey of analysts, and they don't always match. On one Netflix quarter, StreetAccount had 2.73 million new members expected and FactSet had 2.8 million. On Meta's next-quarter revenue, Refinitiv had $27.1 billion and Bloomberg's story $27.3 billion. When the gap between actual and estimate is wide, it won't matter. On a close call, it can flip your verdict. So check whose number you're reading.
questions.lesson_line: Know whose consensus you're reading. On a close call, the survey can flip the verdict.
questions.simple: True. Each outlet quotes its own survey of analysts, and the surveys don't always match.

questions.q: Nike's fiscal Q4 2024 release says results 'led us to update our Fiscal '25 outlook.' No new numbers follow. Where do you get them?
questions.why: The earnings call. Nike's release only said the outlook changed. The numbers came that afternoon, when finance chief Matthew Friend walked analysts through the cut. Schwab says the same: if the guide isn't in the release, check the materials around it or wait for the call. Don't skip it, because guidance can often be the top factor in the near-term price. In our app, open the name from the earnings calendar and check the Call tab for the recap and transcript.
questions.lesson_line: The guide isn't always in the release. When it's missing, go to the call.

wrong.The consensus estimate: That's the analysts' average guess, never the company's own forecast.
wrong.The after-hours price: Price shows you how the market reacted. It doesn't tell you what Nike forecast.
wrong.Last quarter's release: That was written a quarter ago. It can't hold the outlook Nike just changed.

questions.simple: On the earnings call, because that's where Nike's finance chief gave analysts the new outlook the same day.

questions.q: When a company gives its own forecast for a number, you judge the quarter against that forecast too, not just the consensus.
questions.why: True. There are two bars. The Street's consensus is one. The company's own forecast is the other, and I weigh it heavily. Management knows its business better than any analyst, so missing its own number stings. Netflix told everyone it would add 2.5 million paid members. It lost 0.2 million instead, and its own letter printed that right next to the forecast. Schwab lists missing guidance as one way a company disappoints shareholders. Check both bars, every quarter.
questions.lesson_line: Two bars to clear: the analysts' number and the company's own. Check both.
questions.simple: True. A company that sets its own target gets measured against it, and Netflix fell far short of its own.

questions.q: Alphabet, first quarter 2024: EPS of $1.89. The LSEG consensus was $1.51. What's the surprise, in percent?
questions.why: 25.2%. Take the gap first: $1.89 minus $1.51 is 0.38. Divide that by the consensus, $1.51, not by the actual. Times 100, that's 25.2%. Positive, so it's a beat, and a big one. Working it in percent puts a mega cap and a small name on one scale. Then you can tell a real surprise from a rounding error. You don't have to do it by hand, either. Open the name from the earnings calendar in our app. The Earnings History tab lists actual against estimate, with the surprise for every quarter.
questions.lesson_line: Work every surprise in percent, off the consensus. Then any two reports read on one scale.
questions.simple: 25.2%, because the gap of $1.89 minus $1.51 is divided by the $1.51 estimate.

deeper.example: Zacks writes the formula as actual minus consensus, over the absolute value of the consensus, times 100. The absolute value only matters when analysts expect a loss. Every consensus in this lesson is a profit, so the plain form works.

questions.q: Netflix guided to adding 2.5 million paid members in Q1 2022. It lost 0.2 million instead. How far short of its own number was it?
questions.why: 2.7 million. Going from plus 2.5 million to minus 0.2 million, you add the two: 2.5 plus 0.2 is 2.7. That's a miss against Netflix's own guide, and its first drop in paid users in more than a decade. Subscriber growth had long been the key number for this stock. StreetAccount's analysts wanted even more, 2.73 million adds. When a company misses the number it set itself, I take that seriously.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the miss against the company's own forecast too. Netflix missed its own badly.
questions.simple: 2.7 million, because it planned to add 2.5 million and lost 0.2 million, so you add the two.

questions.q: Meta, fourth quarter 2022: revenue $32.17 billion, down 4% from a year ago. Analysts expected $31.53 billion. How does revenue read?
questions.why: A beat, though sales fell. $32.17 billion came in over the $31.53 billion Refinitiv estimate, so revenue beat. The 4% drop from a year ago is growth, a different test. Keep the two apart. The analysts already had sales shrinking, and Meta did better than they feared. Bloomberg said the same: sales fell and still beat. When Meta jumped the next day, Morningstar tied it to this revenue beat.
questions.lesson_line: Growth compares with last year. Beat or miss compares with the estimate. Keep them apart.

wrong.A miss, because sales fell: Falling from a year ago is a growth question. Against the $31.53 billion estimate, it beat.
wrong.In line with last year: In line means it matched the estimate. Sales were down 4% on last year and above the estimate.
wrong.Can't tell without EPS: Revenue gets read on its own line. All you need is the actual and the estimate.

questions.simple: A beat, because revenue came in over the $31.53 billion estimate, even though it fell from last year.

questions.q: Walmart, first quarter of fiscal 2023: adjusted EPS $1.30. The Refinitiv consensus was $1.48. How big is the miss, in percent?
questions.why: 12.2%. For Walmart, that's a big miss. The shortfall is $1.48 minus $1.30, which is 0.18, the 18 cents CNBC reported. Divide by the $1.48 consensus, not the actual, then times 100: 12.2%. In Zacks's terms it's a negative surprise, minus 12.2%. CNBC said it missed by a wide margin, and the stock closed down 11.38% that day. Size the miss before you judge it.
questions.lesson_line: Put the miss in percent, off the consensus, so you can weigh it against any other report.
questions.simple: 12.2%, because the 18 cent shortfall divided by the $1.48 estimate comes to about 12.2%.

questions.q: Meta's Q4 2022 EPS was $1.76. Its release says EPS would be $1.24 higher without restructuring charges. What's EPS without them?
questions.why: $3.00. Add it back: $1.76 plus $1.24 is $3.00. That's Meta's own what-if number, with the $4.20 billion of restructuring charges taken out. The reported EPS is still $1.76. I work both, because the estimate you're about to compare against may have been built on either one. That's the next thing you check.
questions.lesson_line: When a big charge sits in EPS, work the number without it too. Then compare.
questions.simple: $3.00, because you add the $1.24 the charges took off back onto the reported $1.76.

questions.story: Nike, fiscal Q4 2024: adjusted EPS $1.01 vs 83 cents expected. Revenue $12.61 billion vs $12.84 billion expected. It guides fiscal 2025 sales down mid-single digits. Analysts expected a 0.9% rise.
questions.q: If you held Nike into this, which line worries you most?
questions.why: The full-year sales guide. Analysts had fiscal 2025 sales up 0.9%, and Nike told them down mid single digits. That marks down a whole year. The EPS beat and the revenue miss are about a quarter that's already gone. Schwab says guidance can often be the top factor in the near-term price. Our rule: hold through a report only when the trade's up 5R. Nike plunged nearly 20% the next day, and CNBC tied it to the cut.
questions.lesson_line: Read the guide before you celebrate the beat. The beat is last quarter. The guide is the year ahead.

wrong.The adjusted EPS line: It beat, $1.01 against 83 cents. And it's about the quarter that's done.
wrong.The quarter's revenue miss: It matters, but it's one quarter. The guide marks down the whole year ahead.
wrong.Nothing, EPS beat the estimate: A beat doesn't cancel a weak outlook. CNBC tied the plunge to the guidance cut.

questions.simple: The guide, because Nike now sees sales falling for the year while analysts expected a 0.9% rise.

reasons: the 0.9% and 83-cent consensus figures rest on CNBC alone

questions.q: Walmart, May 2022: a new full-year guide. Sales up about 4%, was 3%. EPS down about 1%, was up mid single digits. What's the read?
questions.why: Sales raised, profit cut. Walmart now sees sales up about 4%, from about 3%. It sees EPS down about 1%, where it used to see a mid-single-digit gain. Sell more, keep less. The CEO blamed food and fuel inflation for squeezing margins and costs. If I own it, the profit line is the one I care about, and that's the one that flipped from growth to decline.
questions.lesson_line: A guide can raise sales and cut profit at once. Read both lines before you call it.

wrong.A raise across the board: Only sales went up. The EPS outlook went from growth to a drop of about 1%.
wrong.A cut across the board: The sales outlook went up, from about 3% to about 4%.
wrong.Neither line really moved: Both moved, and the EPS line flipped from growth to decline.

questions.simple: Sales raised and profit cut, because Walmart now sees sales up about 4% but EPS down about 1%.

questions.q: Target, first quarter 2022: a day after Walmart, adjusted EPS of $2.19. The Refinitiv consensus was $3.07. How deep is the miss, in percent?
questions.why: 28.7%. That's not a miss, that's a hole. Gap first: $3.07 minus $2.19 is 0.88, the 88 cents CNBC reported. Then divide by the $3.07 consensus, not the $2.19 actual. 0.88 over 3.07, times 100, is 28.7%. Walmart's miss a day earlier hurt, and this one ran far deeper. A miss that size says something broke in the business, not that analysts were off by a hair. Target fell nearly 25% that day.
questions.lesson_line: Size every miss in percent before you judge it. This one was deep.
questions.simple: 28.7%, because the 88 cent shortfall divided by the $3.07 estimate comes to about 28.7%.

questions.story: Walmart, first quarter of fiscal 2023. Revenue: $141.57 billion vs $138.94 billion expected. Adjusted EPS: $1.30 vs $1.48 expected.
questions.q: What's that mix telling you about the quarter?
questions.why: Sales held, costs hit profit. Revenue beat, so shoppers kept coming. EPS missed, so the money leaked out between the sale and the bottom line. The CEO said food and fuel inflation hit margins and costs harder than expected. AP named labor, fuel and inventory. It's not a one-off charge either. Walmart's adjusted EPS only strips out swings on its equity investments, and what everyone pointed at were everyday running costs. Running costs can stick around, so my next question is whether they carry into next quarter. The stock closed down 11.38% that day.
questions.lesson_line: A sales beat with a profit miss points at costs. Find which ones, and whether they'll last.

wrong.Shoppers pulled back sharply: Revenue beat the estimate, so shoppers kept buying. The squeeze came below the sales line.
wrong.A one-time charge hit EPS: Adjusted EPS already leaves out the investment gains and losses. The miss came from running costs: labor, fuel and inventory.
wrong.A strong quarter all around: Profit missed by a wide margin. A sales beat doesn't make up for that.

questions.simple: Sales held up but costs cut into profit, because revenue beat while EPS missed, and Walmart blamed food and fuel inflation.

deeper.trap: The trap is to read a sales beat as a healthy quarter. Revenue tells you customers came. EPS tells you what was left after costs. When the two split, find the cost first. Walmart's CEO pointed at food and fuel inflation, and AP named labor, fuel and inventory. Then ask whether that cost will last into the next quarter.

questions.story: Netflix, first quarter 2022: EPS $3.53 vs $2.89 expected. Revenue $7.87 billion vs $7.93 billion. Paid members fell by 200,000, against 2.73 million adds expected. It guides to losing 2 million more next quarter.
questions.q: What's the real news in this report?
choices: The EPS beat over the estimate
A currency gain inside the EPS
questions.why: Lost members and the guide. Netflix lost 200,000 paid members where StreetAccount expected 2.73 million added. Then it guided to losing 2 million more. Subscriber growth had long been the key number for Netflix, so this hit the reason people owned it. The EPS beat looks back at a quarter that's done. Members and the guide tell you what's coming. Find the number each stock lives on before you read the headline. The stock plunged 35% in one day.
questions.lesson_line: Find the number each stock lives on. For Netflix in 2022, that was members, not EPS.

wrong.The EPS beat over the estimate: It's real, but it looks back. Members and the guide tell you what's next.
wrong.The slight revenue miss: It missed, but only just: $7.87 billion against $7.93 billion. Variety tied the drop to the subscriber loss.
wrong.A currency gain inside the EPS: The $3.53 did hold a $162 million non-cash currency gain, worth knowing. But members were the key number, and they went the wrong way.

questions.simple: Lost members and the guide, because member growth had long been the key number for Netflix.

deeper.trap: The trap is to lead with the headline line. EPS beat by a wide gap, yet the $3.53 held a $162 million non-cash currency gain, and it says nothing about growth. For Netflix, CNBC called subscriber growth a key metric each quarter. Find the key number for each stock before you read the beat.

questions.story: Meta, fourth quarter 2022: EPS $1.76 vs $2.22 expected. The release says $4.20 billion of restructuring charges sit in that number. Without them, EPS would be $1.24 higher.
questions.q: Before you call EPS a beat or a miss, what do you need to know?
choices: How the stock moved after hours
questions.why: What the $2.22 estimate included. As reported, $1.76 sits under $2.22. Add back the $1.24 the charges took and it clears $2.22. CNBC said the charges made the comparison difficult. You can only compare an estimate and an actual on the same basis. If the analysts built the charges in, compare $2.22 with $1.76. If they didn't, compare it with the number without them. Until you know, I wouldn't call it either way. The stock closed up 23% the next day.
questions.lesson_line: When a big charge sits in EPS, check what the estimate counted before you call it.

wrong.Meta's EPS a year earlier: That's growth, a separate test. Beat and miss compare the actual with the estimate, not with last year.
wrong.How the stock moved after hours: A price shows how the market reacted. It doesn't tell you what the estimate counted.
wrong.Whether revenue beat its estimate: Revenue is its own line. It can't tell you whether the EPS estimate counted the charges.

questions.simple: What the $2.22 estimate counted, because $4.20 billion of charges sit inside the $1.76.

deeper.trap: The trap is to pick a side fast. As reported, $1.76 is under $2.22. Add back the $1.24 and the picture changes. Neither call is safe until you know what the estimate included. Then read the rest of the report: revenue, costs and guidance.

reasons: the key rests on CNBC's judgment plus Fidelity's same-basis rule

questions.q: The bigger a company's EPS beat, the bigger the stock's jump the next day.
questions.why: False. Nike beat, $1.01 against 83 cents. Netflix beat, $3.53 against $2.89. Alphabet beat, $1.89 against $1.51. FINRA says simply beating or missing isn't always what moves a price. The guide and the rest of the report can outweigh it. And remember our rule: no new buys in the 3 days before a report. Three beats, and here's what the stocks did: Nike plunged nearly 20%, Netflix fell 35% in one day, and Alphabet rose 10%.
questions.lesson_line: The size of the beat doesn't set the move. The guide and the rest of the report do.
questions.simple: False. Nike and Netflix both beat, then fell nearly 20% and 35%.

deeper.counter: Netflix is the sharpest case. EPS of $3.53 against $2.89 was a wide beat. Yet the stock plunged 35% in one day, after a revenue miss and a surprise loss of subscribers. A beat on one line can sit beside bad news on the line the market cares about most.

questions.q: A company that reports EPS below the consensus will see its stock fall.
questions.why: False. A miss makes a drop likely, not certain. Meta's reported $1.76 sat under the $2.22 estimate, charges and all. Revenue beat, and Meta lowered its 2023 expense outlook, so the market looked past the EPS line to costs coming down. Weak earnings with upbeat guidance can lift a stock. Read everything under the headline before you decide what it means. Meta closed up 23% the next day.
questions.lesson_line: A miss is likely to hurt, but the rest of the report can outweigh it. Read past the EPS line.
questions.simple: False. A miss makes a drop likely, not certain, and Meta missed yet closed up 23%.

deeper.trap: The trap is the word will. A miss usually sends a stock lower, so the statement feels true. But the price reacts to the whole report. Meta's charges clouded the EPS line, while revenue beat and the cost outlook came down. Read the headline, then read everything under it.

questions.story: May 2022. On Tuesday, Walmart's sales beat but its profit missed. You own Target, and it reports on Wednesday.
questions.q: What does Walmart's report tell you about your Target shares?
choices: Sales beat, so retail is fine
questions.why: A warning about Target's costs. Walmart's sales beat, so its miss came from costs, not lost shoppers. Same kind of store, same kind of costs. A day later Target missed by 88 cents and blamed freight and transportation costs. CNBC said Target's miss confirmed the same story from Walmart. A peer's report is a heads-up, not a sure thing. But if you own Target, this is your heads-up. Up 5R on the trade, you can sit through the report. Not up 5R, we don't hold through earnings anyway, so you're out before it hits. Target fell nearly 25%, and both had their worst days since 1987.
questions.lesson_line: When a bigger name in your group reports a cost squeeze, treat it as a warning for yours.

wrong.Sales beat, so retail is fine: Walmart's sales beat, and its profit still missed. Sales alone miss the story.
wrong.Target should win Walmart's shoppers: Walmart's sales beat, so there's no sign it lost shoppers. Its miss came from costs.
wrong.Nothing, they're separate companies: Separate companies, same kind of costs. Target's miss mirrored Walmart's a day later.

questions.simple: A warning about Target's costs, because Walmart missed on costs, not on sales, and Target may face the same kind.

deeper.trap: The trap is to treat each report alone. A big peer's report is news about the costs your stock may share. Walmart's miss came from costs, not lost shoppers. Target's own release a day later named freight and transportation costs. Weigh the peer read as a warning, never as a sure call on the next report.

questions.story: Two EPS beats. Nike, fiscal Q4 2024: EPS $1.01 vs 83 cents expected, revenue $12.61 billion vs $12.84 billion, full-year sales guided down. Alphabet, first quarter 2024: EPS $1.89 vs $1.51, revenue $80.54 billion vs $78.59 billion, a first dividend.
questions.q: Both beat on EPS. Which one had the problem underneath?
choices: Nike's, revenue missed and guide cut
Alphabet's, a dividend means slow growth
Both, the market sells every beat
Neither, an EPS beat outweighs it
questions.answer: Nike's, revenue missed and guide cut
questions.why: Nike's. Look past EPS and it falls apart. Revenue came in at $12.61 billion against $12.84 billion expected. Then the full-year sales guide got cut to down mid single digits. Alphabet is the opposite. Revenue beat, $80.54 billion against $78.59 billion, and grew 15%. It added a first dividend and a $70 billion buyback on top. Read every line, the same way, for both, before you decide anything. Same EPS headline, opposite next days. Nike plunged nearly 20%. Alphabet rose 10%, its sharpest rally since July 2015.
questions.lesson_line: Two beats, two opposite days. Read past the EPS line before you decide anything.

wrong.Alphabet's, a dividend means slow growth: Revenue grew 15% and beat. A first dividend plus a $70 billion buyback isn't a slowdown.
wrong.Both, the market sells every beat: Not this time. Alphabet's beat got bought, and the stock rose 10%.
wrong.Neither, an EPS beat outweighs it: EPS is one line. Nike's revenue missed and its guide got cut, and it plunged nearly 20%.

questions.simple: Nike's, because its revenue missed and it cut its sales outlook, while Alphabet's revenue beat.

deeper.trap: The trap is to stop at the EPS line, where both reports look alike. Both beat. The difference sits below it. One revenue line missed and one beat. One outlook was cut, while the other company added a dividend and a $70 billion buyback. Read every line the same way for both, then compare.

reasons: Nike's consensus figures rest on CNBC alone

questions.story: Meta guides first-quarter 2023 revenue to $26 billion to $28.5 billion. Refinitiv's consensus is $27.1 billion. Bloomberg News cites an average projection of $27.3 billion.
questions.q: How does Meta's guide stack up against what analysts expect?
choices: A beat, the top end is $28.5B
A miss, the bottom end is $26B
Can't say, a range isn't one number
questions.why: Close. The midpoint sits right between the two. Read a range at its midpoint: $26 billion and $28.5 billion, added and split in half, is $27.25 billion. That's a hair over Refinitiv's $27.1 billion and a hair under the $27.3 billion Bloomberg cited. FactSet scores guided EPS ranges the same way, by the midpoint. Grab the top end and you'll see a beat that isn't there. Grab the bottom and you'll see a miss. Bloomberg called it in line.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a guided range by its midpoint, and know whose consensus you're using.

wrong.A beat, the top end is $28.5B: That's the best case, not the guide. Grab the top end and you'll see a beat that isn't there. Read it at the midpoint, $27.25 billion.
wrong.A miss, the bottom end is $26B: That's the worst case. Read the range at its midpoint, $27.25 billion, and it lands right between the two surveys.
wrong.Can't say, a range isn't one number: You can. Read it at the midpoint, the way FactSet scores guided ranges. Here that's $27.25 billion.

questions.simple: The midpoint is $27.25 billion, just over one survey's $27.1 billion and just under the other's $27.3 billion.

deeper.trap: The trap is to grab the end of the range that fits your view. The top end is the best case and the bottom end the worst. FactSet reads a guided EPS range at its midpoint, so read this one the same way. Then check whose consensus you hold. When the midpoint sits between two surveys, call it close, not a beat or a miss.

reasons: the $27.3 billion average rests on one report whose compiler is not named

conflicts: Survey providers differ. Netflix Q1 2022 subscriber adds: StreetAccount 2.73 million (CNBC) vs FactSet 2.8 million (Variety). Meta Q1 2023 revenue: Refinitiv $27.1 billion (CNBC) vs an average projection of $27.3 billion (Bloomberg via Fortune, compiler not named). q06 and q24 key exactly this. Every beat/miss key uses one named survey as CNBC printed it (Refinitiv in 2022-23, LSEG in 2024), never a mix. Facebook Q2 2018 was considered and left out: secondary reports seen in research put a $1.74 actual against $1.72 (Refinitiv) and $1.75 (Zacks), opposite sides of the line, and I could not verify either on a citable page.

Netflix EPS basis: CNBC writes 'Excluding items, the company earned $3.53', but Netflix reports one diluted EPS ($3.53, GAAP), and its letter says that figure included a $162 million non-cash F/X gain. Whether the $2.89 Refinitiv consensus modelled the gain is unknown. q01 keys only the direction (a beat, by a wide gap); q18 names the gain as a wrong choice, not as the story.

Netflix reaction timing: CNBC Apr 19 'cratered more than 25%' (after hours), Variety 'more than 22%' (after hours), CNBC Jul 19 'plunged 35% in one day' (the next session). Reveals use only the 35% one-day figure, credited to CNBC. CNBC's July story says the drop followed 'a miss on revenue and a surprise loss of subscribers'; q18 keys members as the real news because CNBC's April story and Variety both lead with the subscriber loss and the forecast of more losses, and the revenue wrong-note says it missed.

Meta EPS comparability: the release says EPS would have been $1.24 higher without restructuring charges ($3.00); CNBC says the charges make the $2.22 comparison 'difficult'. Other outlets cite a FactSet estimate of $2.26 (seen in research, not cited). q13 asks only the arithmetic; q19 keys 'unclear', never 'a beat'. q21 calls $1.76 vs $2.22 'reported EPS below the consensus', which is literally true, and the why says why it rallied anyway.

Meta reaction: CNBC 'almost 20%' and Bloomberg 'more than 20%' are after hours on Feb 1, 2023; Morningstar's 'closed up 23% at $188' is the Feb 2 close. Morningstar's page metadata shows 02 February 2023 with a 09:18 UTC stamp, earlier than that day's US close; the text ('Thursday's opening level', 'closed up 23%') only fits a write-up after the Feb 2 close, likely Australian date. Used only in reveals.

Walmart: GAAP EPS $0.74 vs adjusted $1.30; the $1.48 consensus is adjusted (CNBC), so q02, q12 and q17 compare adjusted with adjusted. The guide numbers in q15 are CNBC's wording; the release's guidance table (Feb. 17 vs May 17 columns) shows the same: EPS 'Increase mid single-digits' to 'Decrease about 1%', net sales 'Increase about 3%' to 'about 4%' in constant currency. CNBC also says Walmart fell another 7% the next day; not used.

Target: GAAP EPS $2.16 vs adjusted $2.19; the $3.07 consensus is adjusted. The release rounds revenue to $25.2 billion; CNBC's $25.17 billion is used in questions. 'Fell nearly 25%' is CNBC's report-day figure.

Nike: the release gives GAAP diluted EPS $0.99 and $1.01 excluding restructuring charges; CNBC's $1.01 adjusted matches the latter, so q14/q20/q23 compare $1.01 with the 83-cent LSEG consensus. Other outlets cited $0.84 (seen in research, not cited). The fiscal 2025 guide is not in the release (it says only that results 'led us to update our Fiscal '25 outlook'); CNBC attributes the guide to finance chief Matthew Friend on the call, which q07 keys. CNBC's 'plunged nearly 20% in trading Friday' was updated at 11:11 AM ET Friday; reveals say 'plunged nearly 20% the next day' as CNBC worded it, not a closing figure.
Alphabet: CNBC's Apr 25 headline says shares 'jump 14%' (after hours); the Apr 26 story says they 'shot up 10%' that session and closed at $171.95. Reveals use the 10% session move.
Surprise denominator: Zacks divides by the absolute value of the consensus; every consensus here is positive, so it equals the plain form used in q03, q09, q12 and q16.

Second publishers (checker, 2026-11-09): AP via WKMG ClickOrlando for Walmart (adjusted EPS $1.30 vs $1.48, Zacks survey; sales vs a $138.8 billion projection, a different survey from CNBC's $138.94 billion, a beat either way); AP via News 9 for Target ($2.19 vs $3.07, FactSet poll; AP's $24.83 billion is sales before other revenue, the release's total revenue is $25.17 billion, both beat); Reuters via RTÉ for Alphabet (same LSEG $78.59 billion; 'beat expectations for the quarter in sales, profit'). Nike's 83-cent and $12.84 billion consensus still rests on CNBC alone: other estimates seen in research (84 and 85 cents, $12.86 billion) sit on the same side, so the beat/miss direction holds, and q14/q23 key the guide and the mix, not the consensus figure.
Fortune's Target story (May 18, 2022) says revenue 'was a bit short' while printing $25.17 billion against $24.49 billion expected: an error on its face. Not cited.

Alphabet's $1.89 includes a $0.15 lift from equity-securities gains (release footnote). q04, q09 and q20 use the reported $1.89 as CNBC and LSEG compared it; without the lift EPS is still above every estimate seen ($1.49 Zacks, $1.51 LSEG, $1.53 Bloomberg).

Walmart f54 moved from CNBC to the release (Tier 1): CNBC's sentence mixed this quarter's adjustment with a prior-year divestiture loss. This quarter's adjusted EPS removes one item, equity-investment gains and losses ($0.56).

Meta next-day move: CNBC (Feb 2, 2023, updated 4:00 PM EST) 'jumped over 23% on Thursday'; Morningstar AU 'closed up 23% at $188'. Two publishers agree. Morningstar's piece also says a '$56 billion' buyback and a '$95-100 billion' prior cost range (the release: $40 billion, $94-100 billion), so it is used only as corroboration.

w1.notes: f06 (Investor.gov), f01/f02 (FINRA, Jul 23 2024) and f83 (Zacks) confirmed live, in context. Changed step 1 from 'come in its press release' to 'usually come in a press release, filed with an 8-K': Investor.gov says 'Many companies', not all.
